1	# Facts for #230 (web control surface)
2	
3	No spike was run: every open question needing a browser or iPhone is not runnable here, and none of the rest needs an experiment. `git status` is clean.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	### The tree
8	
9	- A leaked pairing code is short-lived: the window closes on the first successful pairing, after 3 wrong codes, or at 5 minutes. `src/core/remote.rs:46-72` (`Paired` clears `pairing`, "single-use").
10	- `RemoteRequest` is built only inside `src/adapters/remote.rs` (definition `:360`); no test in `tests/` constructs it. Adding `cookie`, `origin` and `user_agent` fields touches the adapter alone. Grep: `RemoteRequest\b` over `src tests`.
11	- `RemoteReply { status, body, authenticated }` is built literally at about 15 sites in `src/app.rs` (e.g. `:1664`, `:2365`, `:2754`, `:3570`, `:3723`, `:3736`, `:3767`) and not in `tests/`. A header field on it needs a `Default` or a constructor, or every site changes.
12	- `RemoteRequest` and `RemoteReply` live in `adapters/`, not `ports/` or `model.rs`, so CLAUDE.md's additivity rule for the shared contract does not name them. `src/adapters/remote.rs:355-393`.
13	- `last_message` exists on the session record: the hook binary writes it from `last_assistant_message` (`src/bin/switchboard-hook.rs:37`) and `src/core/tests.rs:1717` constructs records with `last_message: None`. It is not on the wire: no match in `control/` or `client/Sources`. Adding it to `SessionView` is a new field there.
14	- The certificate can be reissued over the same key. `rcgen::KeyPair::from_pem` is already used at `src/adapters/remote.rs:139,146`, the SPKI hash is of the key (`:107`), and `make_identity` (`:95-127`) is the only path that makes a new key. A reissue keeps `spki_sha256`.
15	- `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`, `BrowserView.swift`, `switchboard-remote/main.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. `addresses` is read as a list at `ConnectionManager.swift:483` and built as a one-element list at `main.swift:120`. A URL parser can fill `addresses` with the one host:port.
16	
17	### Outside the tree
18	
19	- **Apple's TLS server certificate rules.** SHA-2 signature, RSA at least 2048 bits, the server's DNS name in subjectAltName (CommonName not trusted), and for certificates issued after 1 July 2019 an EKU of `serverAuth` and a validity of at most 825 days. Non-compliant connections fail and "websites [may] not load in Safari". Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15; Citrix says iOS 14 / macOS 11 also). The page does not mention IP-address SANs, user-added roots, or exemptions. The current certificate has no SAN, a CN only, and a not-after of year 4096 (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`), so it meets none of the SAN, EKU or validity rules.
20	- **Safari and `wss://` after a click-through.** The behaviour exists and is unfixed: WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is open, status NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, and the reporter got `wss` working only after marking the certificate always-trusted (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419). code-server's iPad doc agrees: Safari "will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile", needs a domain name rather than a bare IP, and needs a SAN matching the host (https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md). Two sources agree; they cover Safari up to 2026-01. One more report is mixed: on iOS 26 beta 3, `wss` failed after acceptance and the poster said it was resolved in beta 5 (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842). That is a forum post, a lead only.
21	  - Queries: "Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate accepted exception fails fetch works"; "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address proceed certificate warning".
22	- **Secure contexts.** `crypto.randomUUID()` is available only in secure contexts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID). The spec decides trustworthiness by the origin's scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", with no mention of certificate errors (https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1; MDN Secure_Contexts agrees). By the text, an https page on a click-through certificate is a secure context. Whether browsers also treat it so is not stated, and it is under Unresolved.
23	- **Cookies are not isolated by port.** RFC 6265 says so, quoted on https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies. `Secure` cookies are sent only over HTTPS. `localStorage` is per origin including port (MDN, general). This confirms the notes' cross-port claim.
24	- **WebSocket subprotocol (RFC 6455 §4.1, §4.2.2, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455).**
25	  - The client must fail if the 101 names a subprotocol it did not offer.
26	  - The server's reply is one `token`, and an empty value is illegal.
27	  - Offered values are `token`s, so base64url without padding is legal. Base64 `=` is not a token character (a separator).
28	  - Whether the client must fail when the server returns none is not normative: §4.2.2 says the server sends none when it agrees to none, and §1.9 (non-normative) says it must include it.
29	  - Browsers must send `Origin` on the handshake. A server may validate it, and rejects with 403. "If the server does not validate the origin, it will accept connections from anywhere."
30	  - The tree's `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) echoes no subprotocol.
31	- **`history.replaceState` replaces the current entry**; Back then shows the new URL and bypasses the old one (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState). It says nothing about what the browser recorded before the script ran.
32	  - Query: "MDN history.replaceState".
33	
34	## Unresolved
35	
36	Each line ends with what the plan builds to. The plan never waits on a line here.
37	
38	1. **Does a click-through exception cover `wss://` and `fetch` on current iOS Safari, with this no-SAN certificate on a bare IP?**
39	   - Tried: the queries above, plus "Safari remember certificate exception visit this website how long self-signed iOS per session". The only evidence is old (2010 bug, iOS 7 and 13 era), the code-server doc (v3.7, 2021), and the one iOS 26 beta post. Nothing current and primary exists.
40	   - Favourable: the page may use the events socket directly. Unfavourable, and the plan must do this anyway: the page works with REST polling alone (poll `changed`-equivalent reads on a timer) and treats the socket as an upgrade it may lose, saying "live updates unavailable" rather than failing.
41	   - Reissuing the certificate with a SAN, `serverAuth` and a bounded validity over the same key is cheap and helps in both cases (Apple's page; the code-server doc).
42	2. **Does a SAN with an IP address, rather than a DNS name, satisfy Safari and Chrome?** The Apple page speaks only of DNS names. Queries: as in 1, plus "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address". No primary source found.
43	   - Favourable: put the LAN IP in the SAN. Unfavourable: the page's URL host must be a `.local` name. Either way the plan reissues with the `.local` hostname as a DNS SAN as well.
44	3. **Does Apple's 825-day rule apply to a manually trusted self-signed leaf?** The page lists no exemption and no scope. Build to a validity of 825 days or fewer and say in the dialog that the certificate is renewed (the key, and so the pin, is unchanged). If it does not apply, nothing is lost.
45	4. **Does a click-through certificate give a secure context in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** The spec reads yes by scheme, but I found no browser documentation on certificate-error overrides. The plan uses `crypto.randomUUID` only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a fallback id generator built on `getRandomValues`, and does not rely on `Secure` cookies being stored without a manual test (see item 5).
46	5. **Are `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake, and do `Secure` cookies work on an IP host, in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** Query: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent on same-origin WebSocket handshake; Secure cookie IP address host Safari Chrome Firefox". Results were blogs and a Chromium design thread (WebSocket requests carry cookies; `wss` counts as the same scheme as `https`): leads, not evidence. Plan to either transport behind one server-side reader that accepts the bearer header, the cookie and the subprotocol token, and let the first manual run pick the page's transport.
47	6. **Is the code-bearing URL recorded in history, tab list or iCloud tab sync before `replaceState` runs?** No source. The plan assumes yes: the code is single-use and the window is 5 minutes or 3 failures (settled above), so a recorded URL is dead once pairing succeeds. The plan says that in the dialog and keeps the query out of server logs (`refuse`, `src/app.rs:3754`, logs path only).
48	7. **Per-site exception lifetime across launches, and loss when the IP changes.** Query: "Safari remember certificate exception ... how long". Only a 2013 blog (iOS 7: exception not removable). Plan: an address change means another warning, and the page and dialog say so. A `.local` name or a reissue never makes it worse.
49	8. **Pool of 4 under a real page load (iOS Safari parallel connections, keep-alive, `/favicon.ico`).** No source for the connection count; it needs a device. Plan: answer static paths on the connection thread with `Connection: close`, serve the page as few files as possible (HTML plus one script and one stylesheet, inlined where possible by the CSP), and give static paths their own bound so a page load cannot starve `/pair`.
50	9. **Bonjour `.local` resolution from iOS Safari.** No query run, so no evidence. Plan: the URL carries the IP from `local_address()` and the `.local` name only if the owner answers item B below.
51	
52	## For the owner
53	
54	A. **On a real iPhone/iPad, after accepting the warning, does the page load, do `fetch` calls work, and does `new WebSocket("wss://…")` connect, with the current certificate and with the reissued one?** Ask with the page as built. Favourable branch: use the socket. Unfavourable: ship polling. The plan builds the polling path regardless.
55	B. **Does `https://<mac-name>.local:<port>/` resolve from the owner's phone?** Favourable: reissue with that DNS SAN and put it in the URL. Unfavourable: the IP stays the URL host. Reissuing with both works either way.
56	C. **Does the owner's phone camera open the URL straight into Safari, and does the tab appear in iCloud tab sync or history before the page script runs?** Either branch: the code is single-use and expires, so the plan holds.
57	D. **Does a cookie, or a subprotocol token, work in Safari with the owner's certificate (items 5, 1)?** Favourable: use the one that works, the cookie preferred for the token never being readable by script. Unfavourable: use the other; the server accepts all three transports regardless.

- **Safari and `wss://` after a click-through.** The behaviour exists and is unfixed: WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is open, status NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, and the reporter got `wss` working only after marking the certificate always-trusted (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419). code-server's iPad doc agrees: Safari "will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile", needs a domain name rather than a bare IP, and needs a SAN matching the host (https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md). Two sources agree; they cover Safari up to 2026-01. One more report is mixed: on iOS 26 beta 3, `wss` failed after acceptance and the poster said it was resolved in beta 5 (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842). That is a forum post, a lead only.
  - Queries: "Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate accepted exception fails fetch works"; "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address proceed certificate warning".
- **Secure contexts.** `crypto.randomUUID()` is available only in secure contexts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID). The spec decides trustworthiness by the origin's scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", with no mention of certificate errors (https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1; MDN Secure_Contexts agrees). By the text, an https page on a click-through certificate is a secure context. Whether browsers also treat it so is not stated, and it is under Unresolved.
- **Cookies are not isolated by port.** RFC 6265 says so, quoted on https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies. `Secure` cookies are sent only over HTTPS. `localStorage` is per origin including port (MDN, general). This confirms the notes' cross-port claim.
- **WebSocket subprotocol (RFC 6455 §4.1, §4.2.2, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455).**
  - The client must fail if the 101 names a subprotocol it did not offer.
  - The server's reply is one `token`, and an empty value is illegal.
  - Offered values are `token`s, so base64url without padding is legal. Base64 `=` is not a token character (a separator).
  - Whether the client must fail when the server returns none is not normative: §4.2.2 says the server sends none when it agrees to none, and §1.9 (non-normative) says it must include it.
  - Browsers must send `Origin` on the handshake. A server may validate it, and rejects with 403. "If the server does not validate the origin, it will accept connections from anywhere."
  - The tree's `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) echoes no subprotocol.
- **`history.replaceState` replaces the current entry**; Back then shows the new URL and bypasses the old one (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState). It says nothing about what the browser recorded before the script ran.
  - Query: "MDN history.replaceState".

## Unresolved

Each line ends with what the plan builds to. The plan never waits on a line here.

1. **Does a click-through exception cover `wss://` and `fetch` on current iOS Safari, with this no-SAN certificate on a bare IP?**
   - Tried: the queries above, plus "Safari remember certificate exception visit this website how long self-signed iOS per session". The only evidence is old (2010 bug, iOS 7 and 13 era), the code-server doc (v3.7, 2021), and the one iOS 26 beta post. Nothing current and primary exists.
   - Favourable: the page may use the events socket directly. Unfavourable, and the plan must do this anyway: the page works with REST polling alone (poll `changed`-equivalent reads on a timer) and treats the socket as an upgrade it may lose, saying "live updates unavailable" rather than failing.
   - Reissuing the certificate with a SAN, `serverAuth` and a bounded validity over the same key is cheap and helps in both cases (Apple's page; the code-server doc).
2. **Does a SAN with an IP address, rather than a DNS name, satisfy Safari and Chrome?** The Apple page speaks only of DNS names. Queries: as in 1, plus "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address". No primary source found.
   - Favourable: put the LAN IP in the SAN. Unfavourable: the page's URL host must be a `.local` name. Either way the plan reissues with the `.local` hostname as a DNS SAN as well.
3. **Does Apple's 825-day rule apply to a manually trusted self-signed leaf?** The page lists no exemption and no scope. Build to a validity of 825 days or fewer and say in the dialog that the certificate is renewed (the key, and so the pin, is unchanged). If it does not apply, nothing is lost.
4. **Does a click-through certificate give a secure context in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** The spec reads yes by scheme, but I found no browser documentation on certificate-error overrides. The plan uses `crypto.randomUUID` only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a fallback id generator built on `getRandomValues`, and does not rely on `Secure` cookies being stored without a manual test (see item 5).
5. **Are `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake, and do `Secure` cookies work on an IP host, in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** Query: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent on same-origin WebSocket handshake; Secure cookie IP address host Safari Chrome Firefox". Results were blogs and a Chromium design thread (WebSocket requests carry cookies; `wss` counts as the same scheme as `https`): leads, not evidence. Plan to either transport behind one server-side reader that accepts the bearer header, the cookie and the subprotocol token, and let the first manual run pick the page's transport.
6. **Is the code-bearing URL recorded in history, tab list or iCloud tab sync before `replaceState` runs?** No source. The plan assumes yes: the code is single-use and the window is 5 minutes or 3 failures (settled above), so a recorded URL is dead once pairing succeeds. The plan says that in the dialog and keeps the query out of server logs (`refuse`, `src/app.rs:3754`, logs path only).
7. **Per-site exception lifetime across launches, and loss when the IP changes.** Query: "Safari remember certificate exception ... how long". Only a 2013 blog (iOS 7: exception not removable). Plan: an address change means another warning, and the page and dialog say so. A `.local` name or a reissue never makes it worse.
8. **Pool of 4 under a real page load (iOS Safari parallel connections, keep-alive, `/favicon.ico`).** No source for the connection count; it needs a device. Plan: answer static paths on the connection thread with `Connection: close`, serve the page as few files as possible (HTML plus one script and one stylesheet, inlined where possible by the CSP), and give static paths their own bound so a page load cannot starve `/pair`.
9. **Bonjour `.local` resolution from iOS Safari.** No query run, so no evidence. Plan: the URL carries the IP from `local_address()` and the `.local` name only if the owner answers item B below.

## For the owner

A. **On a real iPhone/iPad, after accepting the warning, does the page load, do `fetch` calls work, and does `new WebSocket("wss://…")` connect, with the current certificate and with the reissued one?** Ask with the page as built. Favourable branch: use the socket. Unfavourable: ship polling. The plan builds the polling path regardless.
B. **Does `https://<mac-name>.local:<port>/` resolve from the owner's phone?** Favourable: reissue with that DNS SAN and put it in the URL. Unfavourable: the IP stays the URL host. Reissuing with both works either way.
C. **Does the owner's phone camera open the URL straight into Safari, and does the tab appear in iCloud tab sync or history before the page script runs?** Either branch: the code is single-use and expires, so the plan holds.
D. **Does a cookie, or a subprotocol token, work in Safari with the owner's certificate (items 5, 1)?** Favourable: use the one that works, the cookie preferred for the token never being readable by script. Unfavourable: use the other; the server accepts all three transports regardless.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"

schema.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
1	# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)
2	
3	Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at 7fe8949. The facts file
4	is cited as `facts.md` with its section; "Settled" lines are used as
5	written, "Unresolved" and "For the owner" lines are named where a decision
6	rests on one.
7	
8	The default everywhere below is the design that works whichever way the
9	open questions are answered: the page pairs and reads over `fetch` with a
10	bearer header, and treats the events socket as an upgrade it may lose. The
11	cookie transport and the socket are built, and switch on by a constant
12	once the owner has run the page on a phone.
13	
14	## Where this departs from the issue
15	
16	- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows" does not exist.** The notes and
17	  `facts.md` (Settled, The tree) say `last_message` is on the session
18	  record. It is not. It is a field of the hook event
19	  `EventKind::Stopped { last_message, .. }` (`src/ports/events.rs:24`) and
20	  the core drops it: `src/core/events.rs:132` matches
21	  `Stopped { pending, .. }`. `SessionRecord` has no such field and
22	  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`) has none either. So the
23	  list shows what the wire has: kind, `card` (the card's word), `waiting`
24	  and `waiting_reason`. The last response appears only in the session view.
25	  No new read model, no `SessionView` field, no fixture change.
26	- **"The device's scope in the header" has no source after pairing.** No
27	  endpoint returns it (`remote_info`, `src/app.rs:3568`, is unauthenticated).
28	  The page keeps the scope from the `/pair` reply and corrects it when a
29	  `send` is refused with code `scope` (`src/app.rs:3166-3171`).
30	- **"Revoked" cannot be told from "never paired" by the code.** Both
31	  refusals in `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3152`) are `unauthorized`.
32	  The page keeps a non-secret marker (server id, key hash, device id, name,
33	  scope). A 401 with a marker says "this device is no longer paired"; a
34	  401 without one says "open the pairing window on the host". The host
35	  adds no code.
36	- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused" is true, but late.**
37	  `serve_remote` does it (`src/app.rs:3023`) after the request took a slot
38	  in the frame's inbox of 64. The static paths and the 404 for every other
39	  non-API path are now answered on the connection thread.
40	- **§5's relay sentence does not hold for a browser.**
41	  `docs/remote-client.md` §5 says the host's own key check in `/pair` makes
42	  a relayed request fail. `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3636`) compares the
43	  key in the request body, and under a relay the body comes from the
44	  impostor's page. The page's `key` check catches a genuine page talking to
45	  the wrong genuine host (another installation at that address, a rotated
46	  key). It cannot see the certificate it is on. The spec text is amended
47	  to say so.
48	- **`facts.md` says `RemoteReply` is built at about 15 sites.** The tree
49	  has 11 struct literals: ten in `src/app.rs` (`:1664`, `:1679`, `:2365`,
50	  `:2371`, `:2376`, `:2754`, `:3570`, `:3723`, `:3736`, `:3767`) and one in
51	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:829`. No file under `tests/` builds one.
52	- **An existing test changes.** `tests/ui.rs:7474-7490` parses the copied
53	  invite as JSON; it becomes a URL.
54	
55	Decisions the issue asks the plan to settle:
56	
57	1. **Trust: the click-through is the trust step, said in the dialog; the
58	   certificate is not offered for download.** A download only helps if the
59	   device then trusts a manually installed certificate, which needs the
60	   certificate to meet Apple's rules (`facts.md`, Settled, Apple's TLS
61	   rules; the tree confirms the current one meets none of SAN, `serverAuth`
62	   or 825 days: `make_identity`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:102-110`). Whether
63	   Safari lets the owner proceed at all, and whether the exception then
64	   covers `fetch` and `wss`, is Unresolved 1 and 2 and For the owner A; the
65	   plan does not wait on them. It reissues the certificate over the same
66	   key with the IP and the `.local` name as SANs, `serverAuth` and a
67	   validity of at most 825 days (Unresolved 1, 2, 3: helps in every
68	   branch, costs nothing if unneeded). A profile or a download is a later
69	   issue if A says the click-through is not enough. §5's rule becomes: no
70	   non-loopback bind serves anything but `/info`, `/pair` and the page's
71	   three files before pairing; the files are the same bytes for everyone
72	   and carry no secret.
73	2. **Token transport: the bearer header on `fetch`, a subprotocol value on
74	   the socket, the cookie built behind them.** The default needs no browser
75	   behaviour that `facts.md` leaves open: headers on `fetch` work
76	   everywhere, and a base64url token is a legal subprotocol token (Settled,
77	   RFC 6455). The cookie needs Unresolved 5 and For the owner D to be
78	   favourable, so it is the enhancement (`TRANSPORT` in `app.js`, `'token'`
79	   by default). The token sits in `localStorage` under the default,
80	   readable only by this origin's scripts: the CSP (no inline script, no
81	   external one) leaves the page's own script as the only reader. Under the
82	   cookie it is not stored at all.

119	  (`src/app.rs:2895-2898`), and `bind_remote` has just cleared it.

121	  bind. The pairing dialog says so when `local_address()` is not in
122	  `certificate_names` and names the fix (turn "Local network" off and on,
123	  which rebinds); the page's warning interstitial is then the one the owner

125	- The page keeps one non-secret marker in `localStorage`: server id, key
126	  hash, device id, name, scope, host name. The token is a second entry

129	## The signals
130	
131	No new event. The page speaks the existing protocol: `GET info`, `POST
132	pair`, `GET waiting`, `GET projects`, `GET projects/{id}/sessions`, `GET
133	sessions/{id}/last-response` (`screen` for a non-Claude kind), `POST
134	sessions/{id}/send`, `GET ops/{op}`, and the `events` socket with `watch`
135	frames for the content key (`conversation` for `last-response`, `screen`).
136	
137	- **Reads and revisions.** Subscribe first, then snapshot (§4.4). Each
138	  reply carries `epoch` and `revision`; a reply older than what the page
139	  holds for that resource is dropped, a new `epoch` refetches everything,
140	  `resync_required` reconnects and refetches.
141	- **Polling is the floor, the socket the upgrade** (`facts.md`
142	  Unresolved 1; the plan never waits on it). The list and the open
143	  session are refetched every 3 s when no socket is connected and every 30
144	  s when one is (§4.4's visible-view refetch). A socket that fails to
145	  open, or closes, shows "live updates unavailable" and the page carries
146	  on polling; it retries the socket every 30 s. Acceptance step 4 (a
147	  session moves to the top without a reload) therefore holds on either
148	  branch, within 3 s without the socket and at once with it.
149	- **Operation ids.** `crypto.randomUUID()` only when
150	  `window.isSecureContext`, else 16 bytes of `getRandomValues` as hex
151	  (Unresolved 4). A `send` that times out is checked with `GET ops/{op}`,
152	  never resent (§4.5).
153	- **The pairing URL.**
154	  `https://<ip>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`, an
155	  IPv6 host in brackets. The host part is the outward IP from
156	  `local_address()`; the `.local` name goes in only if the owner answers
157	  For the owner B favourably, a one-line change in the dialog, since the
158	  certificate already covers both (Unresolved 9). On load the page, before
159	  any request: reads the query, calls `history.replaceState(null, '',
160	  location.pathname)`, then `GET /api/v1/info`, then compares `key` with
161	  `spki_sha256` and `id` with `server_id`, and posts `/pair` only on a
162	  match. On a mismatch it says "this is not the host whose code was
163	  scanned" and sends nothing. With a marker whose server id matches but
164	  whose key differs from `/info`'s, it says "identity changed, pair again"
165	  and sends nothing, token included (§5).
166	- **The code in history.** Unresolved 6 and For the owner C: whether the
167	  browser records the URL before `replaceState` is unknown. The plan
168	  assumes it does. The code is single use and the window closes at the
169	  first pairing, three wrong codes or five minutes (`facts.md`, Settled:
170	  `src/core/remote.rs:46-72`), so a recorded URL is dead after pairing; the
171	  dialog says that. The connection-thread handler never logs a query
172	  (`read_request` has already split it off, `src/adapters/remote.rs:495`)
173	  and `refuse` logs path only (`src/app.rs:3762-3766`).
174	- **Static paths, on the connection thread** (the frame does core state
175	  only, §4.1): `GET /` (`text/html; charset=utf-8`), `GET /app.js`
176	  (`text/javascript; charset=utf-8`), `GET /app.css` (`text/css;
177	  charset=utf-8`). Each answers with `Cache-Control: no-store`,
178	  `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`,
179	  `Connection: close`, and `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none';
180	  script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; base-uri 'none';
181	  form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`. No inline script or style,
182	  no external resource. If a browser's `'self'` does not cover `wss:`, the
183	  socket is blocked and the page is on its polling floor, which it already
184	  handles. Other methods on these paths: 405 with `Allow: GET`. Any other
185	  path outside `/api/v1/` (a `/favicon.ico` included): 404 with the
186	  existing `not_found` body, also on the thread. Paths under `/api/v1/`
187	  go to the frame as today.
188	- **Pool and rate (`facts.md` Unresolved 8).** A static request is
189	  answered with `Connection: close`, so its slot in the pool of four
190	  (`MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:567`) is freed as soon as
191	  the reply is written; a page load is three short requests. Static paths
192	  get their own window, `STATIC_PER_MINUTE = 120` in `Limits`
193	  (`:623-639`), so a reloading browser cannot spend `/pair`'s six a minute
194	  or `/info`'s sixty. Whether an iPhone's parallel connections still
195	  overrun the pool at accept (`:699-706`) needs a device; it is on the
196	  owner's run list, and the plan raises no limit on a guess.
197	- **Without a code and without a token** the page says: "Open the pairing
198	  window on the host (Settings, Remote devices, Allow pairing) and scan
199	  its QR code." No code-entry form: pairing needs the key, which only the
200	  link carries.
201	- **Origin.** Cross-site hijack needs an ambient credential, and the
202	  default transports are not ambient. The host still checks `Origin`
203	  where an ambient one is in play: on the events upgrade, and on any
204	  request authenticated by cookie, `Origin` when present must equal
205	  `https://<Host header>` (the same origin by IP, `.local` name or
206	  loopback alike), else 403 `origin`. Native clients send no `Origin` and
207	  are unaffected.

17	### Outside the tree
18	
19	- **Apple's TLS server certificate rules.** SHA-2 signature, RSA at least 2048 bits, the server's DNS name in subjectAltName (CommonName not trusted), and for certificates issued after 1 July 2019 an EKU of `serverAuth` and a validity of at most 825 days. Non-compliant connections fail and "websites [may] not load in Safari". Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15; Citrix says iOS 14 / macOS 11 also). The page does not mention IP-address SANs, user-added roots, or exemptions. The current certificate has no SAN, a CN only, and a not-after of year 4096 (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`), so it meets none of the SAN, EKU or validity rules.
20	- **Safari and `wss://` after a click-through.** The behaviour exists and is unfixed: WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is open, status NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, and the reporter got `wss` working only after marking the certificate always-trusted (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419). code-server's iPad doc agrees: Safari "will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile", needs a domain name rather than a bare IP, and needs a SAN matching the host (https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md). Two sources agree; they cover Safari up to 2026-01. One more report is mixed: on iOS 26 beta 3, `wss` failed after acceptance and the poster said it was resolved in beta 5 (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842). That is a forum post, a lead only.
21	  - Queries: "Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate accepted exception fails fetch works"; "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address proceed certificate warning".
22	- **Secure contexts.** `crypto.randomUUID()` is available only in secure contexts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID). The spec decides trustworthiness by the origin's scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", with no mention of certificate errors (https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1; MDN Secure_Contexts agrees). By the text, an https page on a click-through certificate is a secure context. Whether browsers also treat it so is not stated, and it is under Unresolved.
23	- **Cookies are not isolated by port.** RFC 6265 says so, quoted on https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies. `Secure` cookies are sent only over HTTPS. `localStorage` is per origin including port (MDN, general). This confirms the notes' cross-port claim.
24	- **WebSocket subprotocol (RFC 6455 §4.1, §4.2.2, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455).**
25	  - The client must fail if the 101 names a subprotocol it did not offer.
26	  - The server's reply is one `token`, and an empty value is illegal.
27	  - Offered values are `token`s, so base64url without padding is legal. Base64 `=` is not a token character (a separator).
28	  - Whether the client must fail when the server returns none is not normative: §4.2.2 says the server sends none when it agrees to none, and §1.9 (non-normative) says it must include it.
29	  - Browsers must send `Origin` on the handshake. A server may validate it, and rejects with 403. "If the server does not validate the origin, it will accept connections from anywhere."
30	  - The tree's `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) echoes no subprotocol.
31	- **`history.replaceState` replaces the current entry**; Back then shows the new URL and bypasses the old one (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState). It says nothing about what the browser recorded before the script ran.
32	  - Query: "MDN history.replaceState".

35	
36	Each line ends with what the plan builds to. The plan never waits on a line here.
37	
38	1. **Does a click-through exception cover `wss://` and `fetch` on current iOS Safari, with this no-SAN certificate on a bare IP?**
39	   - Tried: the queries above, plus "Safari remember certificate exception visit this website how long self-signed iOS per session". The only evidence is old (2010 bug, iOS 7 and 13 era), the code-server doc (v3.7, 2021), and the one iOS 26 beta post. Nothing current and primary exists.
40	   - Favourable: the page may use the events socket directly. Unfavourable, and the plan must do this anyway: the page works with REST polling alone (poll `changed`-equivalent reads on a timer) and treats the socket as an upgrade it may lose, saying "live updates unavailable" rather than failing.
41	   - Reissuing the certificate with a SAN, `serverAuth` and a bounded validity over the same key is cheap and helps in both cases (Apple's page; the code-server doc).
42	2. **Does a SAN with an IP address, rather than a DNS name, satisfy Safari and Chrome?** The Apple page speaks only of DNS names. Queries: as in 1, plus "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address". No primary source found.
43	   - Favourable: put the LAN IP in the SAN. Unfavourable: the page's URL host must be a `.local` name. Either way the plan reissues with the `.local` hostname as a DNS SAN as well.
44	3. **Does Apple's 825-day rule apply to a manually trusted self-signed leaf?** The page lists no exemption and no scope. Build to a validity of 825 days or fewer and say in the dialog that the certificate is renewed (the key, and so the pin, is unchanged). If it does not apply, nothing is lost.
45	4. **Does a click-through certificate give a secure context in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** The spec reads yes by scheme, but I found no browser documentation on certificate-error overrides. The plan uses `crypto.randomUUID` only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a fallback id generator built on `getRandomValues`, and does not rely on `Secure` cookies being stored without a manual test (see item 5).
46	5. **Are `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake, and do `Secure` cookies work on an IP host, in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** Query: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent on same-origin WebSocket handshake; Secure cookie IP address host Safari Chrome Firefox". Results were blogs and a Chromium design thread (WebSocket requests carry cookies; `wss` counts as the same scheme as `https`): leads, not evidence. Plan to either transport behind one server-side reader that accepts the bearer header, the cookie and the subprotocol token, and let the first manual run pick the page's transport.
47	6. **Is the code-bearing URL recorded in history, tab list or iCloud tab sync before `replaceState` runs?** No source. The plan assumes yes: the code is single-use and the window is 5 minutes or 3 failures (settled above), so a recorded URL is dead once pairing succeeds. The plan says that in the dialog and keeps the query out of server logs (`refuse`, `src/app.rs:3754`, logs path only).
48	7. **Per-site exception lifetime across launches, and loss when the IP changes.** Query: "Safari remember certificate exception ... how long". Only a 2013 blog (iOS 7: exception not removable). Plan: an address change means another warning, and the page and dialog say so. A `.local` name or a reissue never makes it worse.
49	8. **Pool of 4 under a real page load (iOS Safari parallel connections, keep-alive, `/favicon.ico`).** No source for the connection count; it needs a device. Plan: answer static paths on the connection thread with `Connection: close`, serve the page as few files as possible (HTML plus one script and one stylesheet, inlined where possible by the CSP), and give static paths their own bound so a page load cannot starve `/pair`.
50	9. **Bonjour `.local` resolution from iOS Safari.** No query run, so no evidence. Plan: the URL carries the IP from `local_address()` and the `.local` name only if the owner answers item B below.

input.content:
1. **"`RemoteFiles::load_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:74`) already refuses a newer file" is false, and the `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump rests on it.** Premise: the plan's "The record" section. Support: nothing. The tree contradicts it. `load_identity` is `self.load(IDENTITY_FILE)` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:74-76`), and `load` (`:55-63`) is a bare `serde_json::from_slice`. A grep for `schema_version` in `src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/core/remote.rs` and `src/app.rs` finds one use, which writes the constant at `src/adapters/remote.rs:118`. Nothing reads it back. `Identity` (`src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`) has no `deny_unknown_fields`. So the bump to 2 protects nothing: an older build reads a v2 file, ignores the two new fields, and carries on. CLAUDE.md says "the store refuses to write a newer one", and that is the store's `model.rs` path, not `RemoteFiles`. The plan also says an older file "reads with empty names" and treats that as a decision, but it does not say who checks the version. Fix: either add the check (a new refusal in `load_identity`, which is a behaviour change to name in the contract list), or drop the claim and say the bump is a marker only and that `#[serde(default)]` is what makes old files readable. Don't present the refusal as existing.

2. **`<LocalHostName>.local` has no source.** Premise: "Rehydration" lists `<LocalHostName>.local` among the names the certificate answers to, and "the certificate already covers both". Support: nothing in the facts (Unresolved 9 says no query was run) and nothing in the tree. The only host-name code in the tree is `default_server_name`, which runs `hostname -s` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:303-312`). That is the shell host name, not the Bonjour `LocalHostName`, and the two differ on a Mac whose name was edited in Sharing settings. The advertiser takes `identity.server_name` (`src/app.rs:2999`), which can be user-edited. The plan has to say where `certificate_names()` gets the name: a new `scutil --get LocalHostName` call, or the existing `hostname -s`. It also has to say what happens when the name is empty or contains characters illegal in a DNS SAN (rcgen rejects them), because `bind_remote` would fail on that and the port would not come up at all. A robust default is available: put the `.local` SAN in only if the name passes a DNS-label check, and otherwise leave it out and still bind.

3. **A failed reissue in `bind_remote` is not given a default.** Premise: "`bind_remote` (`src/app.rs:2936`) reissues first". Support: nothing says what happens on error. `bind_remote` is the only way the port comes up, and it already returns `Err` for a missing key (`src/app.rs:2950-2955`). If the reissue fails (a SAN rcgen rejects, a write error on `identity.json`, no `local_address()` at all), then as written the remote port, and with it every paired native client, goes down because of an enhancement the browser page needs. State that a reissue failure is logged and the old certificate is served. The plan treats the reissue as "costs nothing if unneeded", which is true only if it cannot break the bind.

4. **The "click-through is the trust step" decision has no fallback if Safari will not proceed, though the plan's claim of working "on either branch" covers only the socket.** Premise: Decision 1 and the Acceptance paragraph ("None of these steps depends on the socket, the cookie or the `.local` name"). Support: `facts.md` Unresolved 1 asks whether the exception covers `fetch` and `wss`. For `wss` the facts have two sources, WebKit bug 41419 and the code-server iPad doc, that say it does not. For `fetch` and the page load itself there is only the Apple page ("websites [may] not load in Safari", `facts.md` Settled, Apple's TLS rules). That is the same page that says the current certificate meets none of the rules. The plan's polling floor covers a lost socket. It does not cover a page that cannot load, or a same-origin `fetch` that the exception does not carry. Step 1 of the acceptance run is exactly that. The reissue is the plan's only mitigation, and Unresolved 2 and 3 (IP SAN, 825 days) leave it unproven. I did not run new searches. The facts record the queries already tried and the plan adds no new evidence. The fix is small and costs no code: say in Decision 1 that if A is unfavourable for the page load itself, the feature does not ship in this cut and the certificate download/profile issue becomes a blocker. Drop "holds on either branch" from the signals section, since the polling claim holds only on the branch where the page and `fetch` work.

5. **"Static paths ... `Connection: close`, so its slot ... is freed as soon as the reply is written" does not follow from the connection loop.** Premise: the "Pool and rate" bullet. Support: `connection` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:770-870`) is a `while let Some(request) = read_request(...)` loop. It frees the pool slot only when the function returns, and nothing in the plan says `respond_static` ends the loop. `respond` writes `Connection: keep-alive` (`:545`), and the loop would go on to the next `read_request` under `IDLE_TIMEOUT`. A header alone frees nothing. The plan's pool test ("four sequential static loads leave the pool free") would pass only if the loop returns. State that `connection` returns `Ok(())` after a static or non-API reply. Also state that the rate check already runs on every request in the loop, so a browser that keeps the connection open and ignores `close` cannot hold a slot.

6. **The `Origin` rule trusts the `Host` header it is meant to check against.** Premise: "Origin when present must equal `https://<Host header>`". Support: nothing in the facts. `facts.md` Settled says only that browsers send `Origin` and a server may validate it (RFC 6455). A page on `https://attacker.example` that DNS-rebinds to the Mac's address sends `Host: attacker.example:<port>` and `Origin: https://attacker.example:<port>`, which satisfy the comparison. It then rides the `SameSite=Strict` cookie only if the cookie is sent to that host, and a cookie is scoped to the host it was set for. So the cookie transport is not exposed. The bearer-transport socket is exposed to nothing, since a page cannot read the token. The check is therefore redundant for the default transport and weak for the cookie, and the plan should not describe it as a hijack defence. Say it compares against the host's own known addresses (`certificate_names` plus loopback) instead of echoing `Host`. That is a stronger check, and the names are already on the record.

7. **"Swift parser keeps decoding JSON ... so `main.swift:111` ... work unchanged" cites lines the plan did not check.** `PairingInvite` is `Decodable` with `parse` at `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`. A grep for `schema_version` in `src/adapters/remote.rs`, `src/core/remote.rs` and `src/app.rs` finds one use, which writes the constant at `src/adapters/remote.rs:118`. Nothing reads it back. `Identity` (`src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`) has no `deny_unknown_fields`. So the bump to 2 protects nothing: an older build reads a v2 file, ignores the two new fields, and carries on. CLAUDE.md says "the store refuses to write a newer one", and that is the store's `model.rs` path, not `RemoteFiles`. The plan also says an older file "reads with empty names" and treats that as a decision, but it does not say who checks the version. Fix: either add the check (a new refusal in `load_identity`, which is a behaviour change to name in the contract list), or drop the claim and say the bump is a marker only and that `#[serde(default)]` is what makes old files readable. Don't present the refusal as existing.

2. **`<LocalHostName>.local` has no source.** Premise: "Rehydration" lists `<LocalHostName>.local` among the names the certificate answers to, and "the certificate already covers both". Support: nothing in the facts (Unresolved 9 says no query was run) and nothing in the tree. The only host-name code in the tree is `default_server_name`, which runs `hostname -s` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:303-312`). That is the shell host name, not the Bonjour `LocalHostName`, and the two differ on a Mac whose name was edited in Sharing settings. The advertiser takes `identity.server_name` (`src/app.rs:2999`), which can be user-edited. The plan has to say where `certificate_names()` gets the name: a new `scutil --get LocalHostName` call, or the existing `hostname -s`. It also has to say what happens when the name is empty or contains characters illegal in a DNS SAN (rcgen rejects them), because `bind_remote` would fail on that and the port would not come up at all. A robust default is available: put the `.local` SAN in only if the name passes a DNS-label check, and otherwise leave it out and still bind.

Support: nothing says what happens on error. `bind_remote` is the only way the port comes up, and it already returns `Err` for a missing key (`src/app.rs:2950-2955`). content.text:
I wrote six numbered objections to `plan.feedback-1.md`. I ran no WebSearch or WebFetch in this round. Every objection rests on the tree or the facts file, with the lines cited in each.

1. **Identity version refusal:** the plan says `load_identity` "already refuses a newer file". It doesn't: `load` is a bare `serde_json::from_slice`, and nothing reads `schema_version` back. The `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump therefore protects nothing as written.
2. **`.local` name:** `<LocalHostName>.local` has no source. The tree only has `hostname -s`, which can differ from the Bonjour name.
3. **Failed reissue:** the plan doesn't say what happens if the reissue in `bind_remote` fails. As written, it could take the whole remote port down for native clients.
4. **Page load:** the "works on either branch" claim covers only a lost socket. Nothing covers Safari refusing to load the page or the same-origin `fetch`, which is Unresolved 1.
5. **Pool slot:** a `Connection: close` header alone doesn't free a pool slot, because the `connection` loop keeps reading until the function returns. The plan never says `respond_static` ends the loop.
6. **Origin check:** the `Origin` rule compares against the `Host` header, so a rebinding page can satisfy it. The plan should compare against the host's known names instead.

The plan's other line references and its `SCHEMA_VERSION` of 16 matched the worktree. Its count of 11 `RemoteReply` literals is also right, against the facts' "about 15". A seventh objection, about Swift callers of `PairingInvite`, was wrong: every caller goes through `parse`. I removed it.
